This homework introduces a few data-wrangling tools that are useful for visualisation.

Main job: **reshape the data so the geom can use it**.

This module is not primarily a data-wrangling module. You do not need to memorise these functions now, but you should recognise why they are useful when a plot needs the data in a different format.

## Load packages and data

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
```

```{r}
blomkvist <- read_csv("data/blomkvist.csv")
blomkvist <- drop_na(blomkvist, smoker, rt_hand_d, rt_hand_nd)
```

## Why reshape data?

Dominant-hand and non-dominant-hand reaction times are currently in separate columns.

```{r}
glimpse(blomkvist)
```

Try this first. It runs, but it does not give us the comparison we really want.

```{r}
# Two separate y variables are awkward for one grouped boxplot.
ggplot(data = blomkvist, mapping = aes(y = rt_hand_d)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_minimal()

ggplot(data = blomkvist, mapping = aes(y = rt_hand_nd)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_minimal()

```

This makes it awkward to compare them in one boxplot. For `geom_jitter()` and `geom_boxplot()`, it is easier if the group labels are in one column and the reaction times are in another column. We can use `pivot_longer()` to put both reaction-time columns into one column.

Complete the column names.

```{r}
hand_rt <- pivot_longer(data = blomkvist,
                        cols = c(___, ___),
                        names_to = "hand",
                        values_to = "rt")
```

```{r}
glimpse(hand_rt)
```

## Plot the reshaped data

Now use the new `hand` and `rt` columns to compare dominant and non-dominant hand reaction times. The data now match what these geoms expect: `hand` is the grouping variable on `x`, and `rt` is the numeric outcome on `y`.

```{r}
ggplot(data = hand_rt, mapping = aes(x = ___, y = ___)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.25, size = 1.5) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.35, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.35) +
  labs(x = "Measure",
       y = "Reaction time (ms)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Filter rows

`filter()` keeps rows that match a condition. For example, the code below keeps participants older than 60.

```{r}
older_participants <- filter(blomkvist, age > 60)
```

Create a plot using `older_participants`.

```{r}
ggplot(data = older_participants, mapping = aes(x = smoker, y = rt_hand_d)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(x = "Smoking status",
       y = "Dominant-hand reaction time (ms)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Select columns

`select()` keeps columns. This is useful when a dataset is large and you only need a few variables.

Complete the code so that it keeps `id`, `age`, `smoker`, and the two hand reaction-time variables.

```{r}
hand_data <- select(blomkvist, ___, ___, ___, ___, ___)
```

```{r}
glimpse(hand_data)
```

## Create a new variable

`mutate()` creates or changes variables. Here we calculate how much slower the non-dominant hand is than the dominant hand.

```{r}
hand_data <- mutate(hand_data,
                    rt_hand_difference = rt_hand_nd - rt_hand_d)
```

Plot the new variable.

```{r}
ggplot(data = hand_data, mapping = aes(x = rt_hand_difference)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 50, fill = "grey70", colour = "white") +
  labs(x = "Non-dominant minus dominant hand RT (ms)",
       y = "Number of participants") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Summary

For visualisation, data wrangling is useful when you need to:

- put variables into a format that `ggplot2` can map easily,
- keep only relevant rows or columns,
- create new variables that answer a clearer question.
